title: Watermelons: Nature's Gift to the World
summary: Josh and Chuck explore watermelons: the Japanese square and heart-shaped watermelons (and the myth that they were made to fit small Japanese refrigerators), watermelon botany (a pepo and berry in the cucumber family), African origins and domestication in Northeast Africa, spread via Egypt, India, China and the Americas, Native American cultivation, Thomas Jefferson and Virginia watermelons, the racist watermelon trope and its history, Charleston Gray variety and disease vulnerability, grafting onto squash rootstock after methyl bromide bans, seedless watermelon development (triploid breeding, Oreste Ruiz/Kihara), production and consumption statistics, growing and ripeness tips, nutrition, pickled and savory watermelon recipes, vodka-infused watermelon, watermelon flavor chemistry, and a listener mail segment from Ian Bowers about running tangents.

segments.title: Opening banter and square watermelon myth
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode and recalls seeing square watermelons. They discuss heart-shaped and pyramid watermelons, and conclude the myth that square watermelons were grown to fit Japanese refrigerators is false because they are grown in containers and are expensive.

segments.title: Watermelon botany and popularity
segments.summary: The hosts discuss watermelon's global popularity, its status as a berry and pepo related to cucumbers and squash, and the species Citrullus lanatus. They debate whether tomatoes are fruit.

segments.title: African origins and domestication
segments.summary: Watermelons originated in Africa. Wild relatives are paler and less sweet and are used for thickening soup, eating seeds, and drinking water. Genetic evidence points to Northeast Africa, possibly Egypt or Sudan, where Nubians may have domesticated the fruit by selecting for sweeter seeds.

segments.title: Spread across the world and to the Americas
segments.summary: Watermelon spread from Egypt across the Mediterranean, reached India by the ninth century CE and China by the tenth century. Spanish colonists brought it to the Americas, and Native Americans grew and traded it widely. The origin of its arrival in America is still debated, including the possible role of enslaved West Africans.

segments.title: Jefferson, Southern watermelons, and the racist trope
segments.summary: Thomas Jefferson grew watermelons at Monticello. Railroad shipping led to varieties that traveled better but tasted worse being sent north. After the Civil War, Black Americans grew and sold watermelons as independent farmers, but white Americans turned watermelon into a racist trope, which persists in media and yard art.

segments.title: Charleston Gray and grafting for disease resistance
segments.summary: Charleston Gray was created by USDA Agricultural Research Service breeder Charles Andrus in 1954 (stated as ninety four in transcript). Nearly all commercial watermelons derive from it, making them genetically similar and vulnerable to pests. The ARS researches hardier watermelons and grafting onto squash rootstock after methyl bromide was banned.

segments.title: Seedless watermelon development
segments.summary: Seedless watermelons come from a manual process using colchicine to make tetraploid plants, crossed with diploid plants to produce sterile triploids. Japanese geneticist Hitoshi Kihara developed the approach, and Oreste (Zanetti) worked to commercialize it, partnering with Sun World International in the late 1980s. Seedless varieties now dominate stores.

segments.title: Consumption, production, and growing watermelons
segments.summary: Americans eat about fifteen pounds per person per year, while Chinese consumption is about a hundred and ten pounds per person. The US grows about two-thirds of its watermelon, with Florida, Georgia, Texas and California leading. Watermelons need about 100 days, space of 18 to 24 square feet per plant, and tips for judging ripeness.

segments.title: Nutrition, recipes, and watermelon flavor
segments.summary: Watermelon is low calorie, mostly water, with some vitamins and lycopene. Grilling and pickling are discussed, along with a watermelon, feta, mint, and pecan salad. Vodka-infused watermelon is considered a myth. The hosts discuss the chemistry of watermelon flavor, which is hard to replicate in candy.

segments.title: Listener mail: Ian Bowers tangents
segments.summary: Listener Ian Bowers lists favorite off-topic tangents from past episodes, and the hosts respond warmly and joke about it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and a mention of watermelon festivals, plus the show credit.
